analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on prescriptions filled by low-income Medicare enrollees.
analysis.headline: The Medicare Drug Savings Act never received a committee vote or any action after its April 2015 referral, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate on prescriptions dispensed to low-income Medicare Part D enrollees, similar to the rebates companies already pay in Medicaid. A manufacturer that refused would have its drugs excluded from Part D coverage. The money would go into Medicare's prescription drug account, lowering federal spending on the program.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicare beneficiaries — mainly people enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, plus other Part D enrollees who qualify for low-income subsidies — would benefit, because drug makers would have to pay the government a rebate on their prescriptions, similar to the rebates drug companies already pay under Medicaid [S2][S3]. The rebates would be deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account, reducing federal Medicare spending and helping finance the drug benefit [S3]. Taxpayers, who subsidize the low-income cost-sharing in Part D, would bear less of that cost [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug manufacturers to pay the government a rebate on every covered drug dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, calculated using the same formula Medicaid uses, so the government stops paying more for these beneficiaries than it does in Medicaid.
Deposits the rebates into Medicare's prescription drug account, reducing the federal cost of the drug benefit and easing pressure on the program's financing.
Excludes the new rebates from Medicaid's 'best price' and 'average manufacturer price' calculations, so the new Medicare rebates do not shrink the rebates states already receive under Medicaid.

Gives the Health and Human Services Inspector General authority to audit manufacturer and plan data, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for late reports and up to $100,000 per false item from plan sponsors.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would pay. They would owe the federal government a rebate on every unit of a covered drug dispensed to low-income Part D enrollees, with the rebate calculated by comparing the Medicaid rebate formula to the discounts the manufacturer already gives through Medicare Part D [S2][S3]. A manufacturer that refused to sign a rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from Part D coverage, losing access to the program's customers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The rebates would be deposited into Medicare's prescription drug account rather than passed directly to beneficiaries, so low-income enrollees' own out-of-pocket drug costs would not go down directly; the gain would show up as reduced federal spending.

Requiring Medicaid-level rebates in Part D reduces manufacturers' revenue on drugs sold to low-income enrollees, which critics argued could lead companies to raise prices for other customers or reduce investment in new drugs; the bill's own design acknowledges this tension by capping the rebate at the amount exceeding the discounts manufacturers already give.

The formula depends on plan sponsors reporting detailed per-drug data and on the Secretary estimating 'average Medicare rebate amounts,' adding administrative complexity and audit burden across every Part D plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted real money — manufacturers' revenue on prescriptions for the poorest Medicare beneficiaries — into Medicare's drug account, at essentially no cost to beneficiaries or taxpayers. Its main design tradeoff is that savings accrue to the government rather than directly lowering low-income enrollees' copays, and manufacturers warned of knock-on price increases. Weighing that against the fact that Medicaid already obtains much lower prices for the same population, the benefit case is strong; the bill's weakness was political, not technical: it was never allowed a vote in either committee that held it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees in April 2015 and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor of Florida, joined by Rep. Sander Levin, introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act of 2015 on April 23, 2015.

The bill would have required drug manufacturers to pay the government a Medicaid-style rebate on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare Part D enrollees, and would have excluded a manufacturer's drugs from Part D coverage if it refused to sign a rebate agreement.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
On April 24 and May 13, 2015, the bill was referred to the Health Subcommittees of those two committees.
No committee or subcommittee action, markup, or vote followed; the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died. They continued selling to low-income Medicare enrollees without paying Medicaid-style rebates, keeping the higher prices the Part D program allows.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and got it referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.

for.name: Rep. Sander Levin
for.what_they_did: Joined Castor in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid-style rebates to the Medicare drug benefit, arguing it would raise premiums for other beneficiaries.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support at any point; the Republican-controlled committees took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required these companies to pay a rebate for every prescription dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, cutting into revenue on the highest-volume government drug program, with exclusion from Part D as the penalty for refusing. Blocking the bill preserved their current pricing.
The bill would have imposed a lower rebate on them than on brand-name manufacturers and required new reporting, but most of the cost fell on brand-name companies.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plan sponsors would have faced new federal reporting duties and civil penalties for late or false reports, but the rebates would come from manufacturers, not plan revenue, so their core role and revenues were untouched.
